1.q: בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת שְׁתַּ֔יִם לְ⁠יוֹאָ֥שׁ בֶּן־יוֹאָחָ֖ז מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מָלַ֛ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ בֶן־יוֹאָ֖שׁ מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה
1.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is introducing **Amaziah** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 8:16.

If your language would not describe a year of a king’s reign in a form such as **the year of two**, you could represent this year in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in the second year of Jehoash]

Here and in verses 23 and 27, the author calls Jehoash by a shortened form of his name, **Joash**, as he also does in 13:25. See what form of the name you decided to use there, and use the same form here and in those verses.

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:17. Alternate translation: [He was 25 years old]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [was Jehoaddan, and she was from Jerusalem]

3.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:13. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be right]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [his ancestor]

4.note: The expression **were not removed** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he did not remove the high places]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [as soon as he had firm control of the kingdom]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [that he killed … the ones having killed]

6.note: The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as Moses wrote in the book of the law]

6.q: לֹא־יוּמְת֨וּ אָב֤וֹת עַל־בָּנִים֙ וּ⁠בָנִים֙ לֹא־יוּמְת֣וּ עַל־אָב֔וֹת כִּ֛י אִם־אִ֥ישׁ בְּ⁠חֶטְא֖⁠וֹ ימות
6.note: The expression **shall not be killed** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You shall not kill fathers for sons, and you shall not kill sons for fathers. Rather, you shall kill a man for his sin]

Here the masculine terms **Fathers**, **sons**, and **man** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. The UST models one way to do that.

7.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he struck** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to put focus on Amaziah as the king who led the Judean army to do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [He was the king who struck]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [he defeated]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:1](ta:01). Alternate translation: [the Edomites]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [where the Israelite killed 10,000 of their soldiers]

It might seem that the expression **called its name** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [And he called it] or [And he named it]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:22. Alternate translation: [and that is still its name at the time of this writing]

8.note: Amaziah is not telling Jehoash to **Come** somewhere. He is saying **Come** to encourage him to take the action that he describes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [Come on]

Amaziah is using **let us see one another’s faces** as a common expression of his culture to mean “let us fight a battle against each other.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [let us meet face to face] or [let us fight a battle against each other]

9.note: To try to make Amaziah realize that he will lose the battle if they fight, Jehoash has his messengers tells him a story. It is a parable, a brief story that teaches something that is true and delivers its lesson in a way that is easy to understand and hard to forget. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state explicitly that the messengers are telling a story. You could also begin this story in the way that made-up stories usually begin in your language. Alternate translation: [and he had them tell Amaziah a story to make him realize he would lose the battle if they fought. They said, “Once upon a time, a thornbush that {was} in Lebanon]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling it to give its daughter to its son as a wife]

By making this request or demand, the thornbush was symbolically claiming to be equal to the cedar, since in the ancient world fathers would only let their daughters marry the sons of men who were their equals. if it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote.

10.note: Jehoash is repeating forms of the verb “strike” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Certainly you have struck]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [Certainly you have defeated]

Jehoash is speaking as if Amaziah’s **heart** had actually **lifted** him up. He is using the heart to represent a person’s feelings, and he is using being lifted to a high position to mean becoming proud. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you are so elated that you have become proud]

The expression **Be honored** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Be content with the honors that come with your victory]

Jehoash assumes that Amaziah will know that by **stay in your house**, he does not mean that Amaziah should not leave his palace. He means that he should not lead his army out to war against him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but do not lead your army out to war against me]

10.q: וְ⁠לָ֤⁠מָּה תִתְגָּרֶה֙ בְּ⁠רָעָ֔ה וְ⁠נָ֣פַלְתָּ֔ה אַתָּ֖ה וִ⁠יהוּדָ֥ה עִמָּֽ⁠ךְ
10.note: Jehoash is using the question form to warn Amaziah and discourage him from fighting. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no reason for you to contend with calamity, so that you will fall, you and Judah with you!]

Jehoash is speaking of **calamity** as if it were a living thing that Amaziah could actually **contend with**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [why should you stir up trouble] or [why should you risk causing calamity for your kingdom]

Jehoash is speaking as if Amaziah and Judah would actually **fall** from a height. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that you will be destroyed, you and Judah with you] or [so that both you and Judah will be destroyed]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 10:6. Alternate translation: [But Amaziah did not do what Jehoash said]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:8. Alternate translation: [and they met face to face] or [and they fought a battle against each other]

12.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [And Judah was struck as it opposed Israel]

The expression **was struck** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Israel struck Judah in this conflict]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [And Israel defeated Judah in this conflict]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:21. Alternate translation: [And their soldiers abandoned the army and returned home]

13.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a distance of 400 cubits]

These **cubits** were a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or about 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this length in modern measurements, either in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The UST models one way to do that.

14.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 12:18. Alternate translation: [that were]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he took sons of pledges]

The author is using the phrase **sons of** to indicate that these people had the characteristic of something. In this case, he means that these people had the characteristic of serving as a guarantee of **pledges** that Amaziah made not to attack Israel. See how you translated the similar expression in 2:16. Alternate translation: [hostages]

15.q: וְ⁠יֶתֶר֩ דִּבְרֵ֨י יְהוֹאָ֜שׁ אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשָׂה֙ וּ⁠גְב֣וּרָת֔⁠וֹ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִלְחַ֔ם עִ֖ם אֲמַצְיָ֣הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֑ה הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
15.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is concluding the story of Jehoash. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in 1:18.

16.note: See how you translated the same expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [And Jehoash passed away] or [And Jehoash died]

The expression **was buried** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people buried him]

18.q: וְ⁠יֶ֖תֶר דִּבְרֵ֣י אֲמַצְיָ֑הוּ הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה
18.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is concluding the story of Amaziah. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in 1:18.

19.note: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And they formed a conspiracy] or [And a conspiracy formed]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. The context suggests that Amaziah’s own officials conspired against him. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And his officials formed a conspiracy]

20.note: Because the author says **the** horses, he probably means Amaziah’s own horses. In that case, he would be using the **horses** to represent Amaziah’s royal chariot, which the horses pulled. Alternate translation: [And they brought him back in his royal chariot]

Bringing Amaziah’s body back to Jerusalem in his royal chariot was a symbolic action by which the conspirators who killed him nevertheless showed respect for his role as king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And they brought him back to Jerusalem respectfully in his royal chariot]

21.note: The author is saying **all** as a generalization. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the meaning. Alternate translation: [And by general agreement the people of Judah took]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:17. Alternate translation: [now he was 16 years old]

22.note: The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [He, he returned Elath to Judah and built it up]

The author is stating the pronoun **He** separately, even though the verb translated as **he built up** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to specify that while it was Amaziah who defeated the Edomites generally (as he describes in 14:7), it was Azariah who reconquered and fortified Elath. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [He was the one who built up]
See how you translated the same expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [after the king passed away] or [after the king died]

23.q: בִּ⁠שְׁנַת֙ חֲמֵשׁ־עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה לַ⁠אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ בֶן־יוֹאָ֖שׁ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה מָ֠לַךְ יָרָבְעָ֨ם בֶּן־יוֹאָ֤שׁ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ בְּ⁠שֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן אַרְבָּעִ֥ים וְ⁠אַחַ֖ת שָׁנָֽה
23.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing **Jeroboam** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Israel**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 8:25 and 13:10.

24.q: וַ⁠יַּ֥עַשׂ הָ⁠רַ֖ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה לֹ֣א סָ֗ר מִ⁠כָּל־חַטֹּאות֙ יָרָבְעָ֣ם בֶּן־נְבָ֔ט אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֶחֱטִ֖יא אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
24.note: The author is continuing to introduce Jeroboam, the son of Jehoash. See how you translated the similar expressions in 3:3 and 8:18. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil. He did not stop committing the same sins as Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin]

25.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 14:22. Alternate translation: [He was the one who restored]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:32. Alternate translation: [the territory of Israel]

25.q: כִּ⁠דְבַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבֶּ֗ר בְּ⁠יַד
25.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [according to the message that Yahweh the God of Israel spoke]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:36. Alternate translation: [through the agency of]

26.note: Here the word **For** introduces an explanation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh enabled Jeroboam to do that because he saw]

26.q: וְ⁠אֶ֤פֶס עָצוּר֙ וְ⁠אֶ֣פֶס עָז֔וּב וְ⁠אֵ֥ין עֹזֵ֖ר לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
26.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he saw that there was and none restrained and none set free and no helper for Israel]

26.q: וְ⁠אֶ֤פֶס עָצוּר֙ וְ⁠אֶ֣פֶס עָז֔וּב וְ⁠אֵ֥ין עֹזֵ֖ר לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, in order to put a general statement before more specific details about it, you may want to put the information that there was **no helper for Israel** before the information that no one **restrained** and no one **set free** was able to help Israel. Alternate translation: [and there was no helper for Israel, none restrained and none set free]

The author is referring to all Israelites by naming the two main categories of them, those **restrained** (legal slaves) and those **set free** (legal free men). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the same expression in 1 Kings 14:10. Alternate translation: [no one at all]

The expressions **restrained** and **set free** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express these ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whether slave or free]

27.note: The author is speaking as if the **name of Israel** were actually written in ink on a scroll somewhere and that Yahweh would actually **wipe** the ink off the scroll. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he would make Israel cease to exist as a nation anywhere on earth]

The word that the ULT translates as **saved** here comes from the same root as the word that it translates as “savior” in 13:5. There, after saying that Yahweh “saw the oppression of Israel,” the author says that “Yahweh gave to Israel a savior.” The similarity of language between that passage and this one suggests that the author meant that Jeroboam was that “savior.” To help your readers make this connection, see how you translated the term in 13:5 that the ULT translates as “savior” and translate the term **saved** similarly here. Alternate translation: [so he delivered them] or [so he rescued them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:36. Alternate translation: [through the agency of]

28.q: וְ⁠יֶתֶר֩ דִּבְרֵ֨י יָרָבְעָ֜ם וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשָׂה֙ וּ⁠גְבוּרָת֣⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁר־נִלְחָ֔ם וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵשִׁ֜יב אֶת־דַּמֶּ֧שֶׂק וְ⁠אֶת־חֲמָ֛ת לִ⁠יהוּדָ֖ה בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
28.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is concluding the story of Jeroboam. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in 1:18.

29.note: See how you translated the same expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [And Jeroboam passed away] or [And Jeroboam died]

Based on how the author usually concludes his stories of Israelite kings, here he has probably left out some of the words that he ordinarily uses. He probably means “and he was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.” See how you translated that statement in 13:13 and 14:16.
